task: I'm putting my square logo on a photo of a mountain sunrise for an Instagram post. The top-left has a bright sky and the bottom-right is dark rock. Where should I place the logo and what size and color should I use so it stays readable?
rewrite:
ambition:     Place the logo by measuring, not by eye. A top brand designer would sample the luminance of the candidate corners, pick the one with the most even tone, and keep the logo off the sunrise focal point and inside Instagram's crop and safe margins (the 3:4 profile-grid crop trims the edges of a 4:5 post).
agency:       The raw material is the exported photo at post dimensions (for example 1080×1350) and the actual logo file with transparency, so the real pixels under the logo can be sampled. Neither is in reach here, so assume the described layout (bright top-left, dark rock bottom-right) and a logo in one dark and one light version.
acceleration: Use the WCAG 1.4.11 non-text contrast threshold (3:1 minimum, higher is better) and an eyedropper or luminance readout in Figma, Photoshop, or Canva. Use a squint or blur test and a downscale to grid-tile size for legibility.
accuracy:     Compute the contrast ratio between the logo color and the sampled background pixels, aiming for 3:1 or higher. Then view the mockup at phone-feed size and at profile-grid thumbnail size, in grayscale, and ideally on a real phone through Instagram's own preview or a draft post. If no preview is available, the closest proxy is the downscaled grayscale view.

Answer as a social media brand designer who places logos on photographs for Instagram. The standard is that a viewer scrolling on a phone can read the logo at feed size without it competing with the sunrise.

I'm putting my square logo on a photo of a mountain sunrise for an Instagram post. The top-left has a bright sky and the bottom-right is dark rock. Tell me where to place the logo, what size to make it, and what color to use so it stays readable.

Give a specific recommendation for each of the three:
- **Placement:** which corner or area, the margin from the edges (as a percentage of image width), and why. Keep it clear of the sunrise focal point and inside Instagram's grid-crop and safe margins.
- **Size:** as a percentage of image width, balancing legibility at phone size against not dominating the photo.
- **Color:** which logo version to use (light or dark, or a reversed or knockout version), judged by contrast against the background it will sit on. Aim for at least a 3:1 contrast ratio.

I have not shared the photo or logo file, so work from the description, state your assumptions, and do not invent details about the image. End with the check: contrast measured by sampling the pixels under the logo, then a view at feed size, grid-thumbnail size, and in grayscale. Finish by naming the one piece of raw material that would sharpen the advice, which is the actual photo and logo file.

answers.plain:
**Placement: bottom-right corner, on the dark rock.** The contrast there is naturally strong, so you can use a light logo and it will pop without any tricks. The bright sky at top-left would wash out most logos.

**Color:** Use a white or very light version of the logo (or the logo on a white square tile). Light on dark rock gives you the best readability. If your logo is multicolor, a white monochrome version is usually cleaner on a photo than the full-color one.

**Size:**
- Make it about **12–18% of the image width**. That's big enough to read on a phone, but small enough not to compete with the sunrise.
- For a 1080 px wide post, that's roughly **130–200 px** square.

**Margins:** Keep the logo about **5–6% of the width (60 px or so)** away from the right and bottom edges. Instagram's grid crop and UI overlays can clip things that sit too close to the edge.

**Tips to keep it readable:**
- Set opacity to **85–100%**. Below about 70%, it can get lost in the rock texture.
- If the rock has busy detail behind the logo, add a very soft, subtle drop shadow or darken that corner slightly (a gentle gradient or burn).
- Check the 4:5 and 1:1 crops, and view it at thumbnail size. If you can still recognize the logo there, it's fine.
- Avoid placing it right at the point where the dark rock meets the bright sky, since the logo would be partly on light and partly on dark.

If the dark area is smaller than expected, or the logo is dark-colored only, put it on a white rounded square tile at around 90% opacity instead. That works on any background.
answers.nudge:
**Put the logo in the bottom-right, on the dark rock, as a white or warm off-white version.**

**Placement**
- The dark rock gives you the highest, most stable contrast. The bright sky is the worst place for a light logo, and a dark logo up there would compete with the sunrise, which is your focal point.
- Keep the logo clear of the bottom edge and right edge by about 6% of the image width. On a 1080 px wide post that's about 65 px. This keeps it out of Instagram's UI overlays (the caption and the like and share buttons on Reels and previews) and out of the grid crop. The grid now shows a 3:4 crop of feed posts, so a logo hugging the edge can get clipped.
- Use the same margin on the right and bottom so it looks deliberate.

**Size**
- Make it about 11–14% of the image width. That's roughly 120–150 px on a 1080 px canvas.
- Go larger only if the logo has fine detail. Below about 100 px, thin strokes and small text break down on phones.
- Judge the size at thumbnail scale (about 300 px wide), not at full resolution. If you can't identify it there, make it bigger.

**Color**
- Use pure white or a warm off-white (about `#F4EFE6`). The warm tint echoes the sunrise light and looks less stuck-on than stark white.
- If the logo is a full-color square tile, keep the tile. Give it a thin light or dark keyline only if the tile's edge disappears into the rock.
- If it's a single-color mark, use the white version. If you only have a dark version, put it on a white tile with slightly rounded corners.
- Keep opacity at 90–100%. Below about 80%, rock texture shows through and hurts legibility.

**Checks before posting**
1. **Texture under the logo.** Dark rock often has bright cracks and highlights. If the area isn't an even dark tone, add a soft shadow behind the logo (about 30–40% black, 20–30 px blur, no offset). Or burn in a subtle dark gradient in the bottom-right corner, using a very low-opacity radial or linear gradient, so the logo sits on a calmer patch.
2. **Contrast.** Sample the brightest pixel under the logo. You want roughly 4.5:1 against the logo color. As a quick test, desaturate the image and see whether the logo still stands out.
3. **Phone test.** View it at arm's length on a phone at low brightness and in sunlight. Dark rock plus a bright screen reflection is where weak logos vanish.
4. **Balance.** A bottom-right logo adds weight to a corner that is already dark. That's usually fine, because the bright top-left sky balances it diagonally. If the horizon or main peak sits low-right, nudge the logo inward slightly rather than crowding it.

**Fallback.** If the rock is too busy or too light for a clean white logo, use a dark logo on the sky in the top-left, with a similar margin. Check that it doesn't overlap the sun or its glow. A dark logo only works there if the sky is clean and the logo clearly separates from it.

If you send me the image and the logo file, I can sample the actual luminance in both corners and composite a test version at a few sizes.
answers.skill:
## Assumptions

- I haven't seen the photo or logo, so this works from your description only.
- I'm assuming a 4:5 portrait feed post (1080×1350), which is Instagram's current default. The profile grid now crops to 3:4, so the left and right edges lose a little. If you're posting 1:1 or 16:9, the numbers still hold, but the safe zones shift.
- I'm assuming the sun and brightest glow sit somewhere in the middle of the frame or along the horizon, not in a corner. You described the top-left as bright sky, so the sun may be near it. Check this first.
- I'm assuming the logo is a simple one- or two-color mark with a transparent background, and that it has a light or dark version, or can be recolored.

## Placement

**Bottom-right, on the dark rock.** Keep the margin at **5% of image width** (about 54 px on a 1080 px canvas) from both the right and bottom edges.

Why:
- The dark rock is the most uniform, lowest-detail area you've described, so a light logo gets a clean, steady backdrop.
- It's far from the bright sky and the sunrise, so the logo doesn't compete with the focal point.
- 5% clears Instagram's grid-crop trimming on the sides. It also keeps the logo out of the bottom strip where the caption gradient, UI overlays and, on Reels or Stories, the interface sit.
- Bottom-right is a conventional spot for a mark, so viewers read it as a signature.

Caveat: if the sun or its glow is close to the bottom-right, or the rock has a bright rim light or snow patch there, move the logo to the bottom-left. Keep the same margin and check the contrast again.

Avoid the top-left. Bright sky there forces a dark logo, and it sits where the eye lands first, so it would compete with the sunrise.

## Size

**14% of image width** (about 150 px on 1080 px). The workable range is 12–16%.

Why:
- A square mark under about 11% (roughly 120 px) turns to mush at feed size, where the image shows at around 375–430 pt wide on a phone. At 14% it's about 55 pt wide, enough to hold fine detail.
- Above about 18% it starts to read as a sticker and pulls attention from the photo.
- At grid-thumbnail size it shrinks to roughly a third of that. If the mark has thin strokes or small text, it will fail there. In that case, use the simplified icon-only version, or go up to 16%.

## Color

**Use the light version: white or a warm off-white, around #FFFFFF to #F5F1E8.** Don't use a dark logo, and don't use a knockout unless the mark is bold.

Why:
- Dark rock will probably sample around L* 10–25. Assuming the rock is near #1A1A1A, white gives about 17:1 contrast. Even if the rock is a lighter #5A5A5A, white still gives about 7:1. Both are well above the 3:1 floor.
- A dark logo on dark rock would fall below 3:1, and a dark logo in the bright sky would fight the sunrise.
- Use a reversed, all-white version of the mark, not the full-color one. Brand colors tend to lose contrast on rock tones, especially blues, greens and browns.
- If the rock has texture or highlights, add a very soft shadow (about 20–30% black, 4–8 px blur, no offset). That lifts legibility without a visible effect. Don't use a hard outline or a backing box.

## Check before posting

1. **Measure contrast.** Sample the pixels under the logo's footprint, taking the average and the lightest 10% of pixels, not just one spot. Compute the contrast ratio between your logo color and those values. Aim for at least 3:1 against the lightest pixels, and ideally 4.5:1 or more.
2. **Feed size.** View the final at about 400 px wide, or on your phone at arm's length. The mark should be recognizable without squinting.
3. **Grid thumbnail.** Shrink to around 135 px wide, or check the real profile grid with the 3:4 crop. Confirm the logo isn't clipped and the mark still reads, even if only as a shape.
4. **Grayscale.** Desaturate the image. If the logo disappears, the contrast is relying on hue, not luminance, and it needs fixing.

## What would sharpen this

The one thing I need is **the actual photo and logo file**, ideally the photo at full resolution and the logo as a transparent PNG or SVG. With them I could confirm where the sun sits, measure the real rock tones under the logo, and tell you whether the 14% size works for your mark's detail.
